title: CDNs: Content Delivery Networks
intro: Your servers might be in one city, but your users are everywhere. A CDN brings content physically closer to them.

slides.heading: The distance problem
slides.subtitle: Data takes time to travel.
slides.explain: A request from Mumbai to a server in the US crosses the world and back. Even over fiber, that distance adds noticeable delay to every file.
points: Every image and script pays the cost

slides.heading: What a CDN is
slides.subtitle: Servers around the world.
slides.explain: A CDN is a network of edge servers in many cities. Users are routed to a nearby edge, which serves a cached copy of your content.
points: The origin is only hit on a cache miss

slides.heading: What to put on it
slides.subtitle: Best for static content.
slides.explain: Files that are the same for everyone are perfect for a CDN. Many CDNs can also cache public API responses and run code at the edge.

slides.heading: Cache control
slides.subtitle: Telling the CDN what to keep.
slides.explain: Cache-Control headers decide how long edges keep a file. Hashed filenames like app.3f9a.js let you cache for a year and still ship updates instantly.
points: Purge the cache for urgent changes

slides.heading: Extra benefits
slides.subtitle: More than speed.
slides.explain: Because edges absorb most of the traffic, your own servers handle far less. Many CDNs also help absorb DDoS attacks.

scenario.situation: A startup serves product images from one server in Mumbai, but many customers are in the US and Europe.
scenario.problem: Overseas users wait seconds for each image, and many leave before the page finishes loading.
scenario.fix: Put the images behind a CDN. Overseas users now load them from a nearby edge server instead of from Mumbai.
scenario.takeaway: Serve static files from close to your users.

cta: Which CDN do you use for your projects?
